content:
We have now studied two of the three animals of the burnt offering. The young bull spoke of Christ’s full strength given in total service and surrender to the Father. The ram spoke of Christ as the substitute; the one caught in the thicket of our condemnation so that the condemned could go free. Today we come to the third animal: one male lamb of the first year. This is the most repeated sacrificial animal in all of the Torah, appearing more times and in more contexts than any other offering. And there is a reason for that. The one-year-old lamb is the clearest, most precise, most consistently used prophetic shadow of Jesus Christ in the entire Old Testament.

The requirement was specific. Not a newborn lamb, still weak and incomplete. A lamb of the first year; in the freshness and strength of its best season, without any mark of age or decay. It was the lamb at the point of its fullness; mature enough to be complete, young enough to be without blemish. The Law was precise about this because the offering had to be the best. Not what was left over. Not what was conveniently available.

This speaks directly of Christ. Peter writes in 1 Peter 1:19 that we were redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” Without blemish; no internal defect of character or nature. Without spot no external mark of sin or corruption. The one-year-old lamb in its fullness is Christ at the height of His perfect humanity, offered to the Father in the complete freshness of an unblemished life. He was not a diminished offering. He was not a tired or compromised sacrifice. He was the lamb of the first year; the best, the full, the complete given wholly.

Of all the places the one-year-old lamb appears in Scripture, the Passover is where the connection to Christ is most direct and most deliberate. Exodus 12:5 gives the Passover requirement precisely: “Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year.” Male of the first year. The same language as Numbers 7:15. The Passover lamb was selected on the tenth day of the first month and kept until the fourteenth day, when all the assembly of Israel killed it at twilight. Its blood was applied to the doorposts and the lintel of every house, and when the angel of death passed through Egypt, every household under the blood was passed over. Death saw the blood and moved on.

John the Baptist declared the fulfilment of this picture the moment he saw Christ approaching the Jordan: “Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Not a lamb of God. The Lamb of God. The one to whom every Passover lamb had been pointing for over a thousand years. 

And Paul states it plainly in 1 Corinthians 5:7: “Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us.” Our Passover. The blood on the doorpost was always His blood in picture form. The angel of death that passed over the blood-marked houses in Egypt was always going to pass over the soul that shelters under the blood of Christ. The lamb of the first year at Passover a prophecy held in animal form, enacted year after year for centuries until the true Lamb arrived.

What makes the one-year-old lamb so remarkable as a type of Christ is not just that it appeared at Passover. It appeared everywhere. Exodus 29:38-39 commanded two lambs of the first year to be offered every single day without exception; one in the morning and one in the evening. Morning and evening, day after day, year after year, the one-year-old lamb was placed on the altar. This was the tamid; the continual offering. The lamb that never stopped being offered. And this continual daily offering points to Christ whose atonement is not a one-day event that fades but an eternal, continual, never-expiring redemption. Hebrews 7:27 says He “did this once for all when He offered up Himself.” One offering. But it covers every morning and every evening of every life that has ever lived. The daily lamb said: this will one day be done once, and the once will be enough for every day.

On the Sabbath, additional one-year-old lambs were offered alongside the daily offering (Numbers 28:9). At every new moon, more lambs of the first year (Numbers 28:11). At Passover, at Pentecost, at the Feast of Trumpets, at the Day of Atonement, at the Feast of Tabernacles; in every feast and every appointed time of the covenant calendar, the lamb of the first year appeared (Numbers 28-29). There was no sacred season in Israel’s calendar that was not marked by the blood and the life of the one-year-old lamb. The entire worship life of God’s people was soaked in the testimony of this one animal because it pointed toward the Lamb of God.

Two more appearances of the one-year-old lamb deepen the portrait further. Leviticus 23:12 commands that when the firstfruits were offered the wave sheaf of the first grain of the harvest brought before Yahweh a one-year-old lamb was to be offered as a burnt offering at the same time. The firstfruits and the lamb together. This connects precisely to 1 Corinthians 15:20: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection. And the firstfruits in Leviticus were always offered with a lamb of the first year. The resurrection of Christ and the sacrifice of Christ cannot be separated. The lamb accompanies the firstfruits because the resurrection is inseparable from the cross.

And in Leviticus 14:10-11, when a person who had been healed of leprosy was to be formally cleansed and restored to the congregation, the cleansing offering included two male lambs of the first year. Leprosy in Scripture is a consistent picture of sin; defiling, isolating, spreading, cutting the sufferer off from the community and from the worship of God. The cleansed leper was restored to full fellowship through the blood and the life of the one-year-old lamb. This is exactly what Christ does for those He cleanses. He does not merely remove the external mark of sin. He restores full fellowship, full access, full standing before the Father. The leper who was outside comes home through the lamb.
Every sinner who was cut off is restored through the Lamb.

The one-year-old lamb of the Torah does not disappear in the New Testament. It arrives. Revelation 5:6 shows us the final vision: “And between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders I saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain.” A Lamb standing. Alive. But bearing the marks of slaughter. The Lamb of Numbers 7:15, the Lamb of Exodus 12:5, the Lamb of the daily burnt offering, the Lamb of Leviticus 14, the Lamb of all the feasts all of them are this Lamb, standing at the centre of heaven, alive from the dead, still bearing the wounds, and standing on our behalf in front of the Father.

Revelation 5:12 says “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing!” The one-year-old lamb of the burnt offering in Numbers 7 was placed on an altar in the wilderness and consumed by fire. The Lamb of God was placed on the altar of the cross and consumed by the full weight of human sin and divine judgment. And now He stands at the centre of the throne, no longer on the altar but on the seat of all authority. The lamb of the first year has become the Lamb who reigns forever.

title: Prayer
text:
Yahweh, from the first Passover night in Egypt to the last page of Revelation, You have been pointing us to the Lamb. Every morning and every evening, the lamb of the first year was placed on the altar day after day, feast after feast, year after year and every time it said: there is one coming who will make this real. We thank You that He came. We thank You that the Lamb of God arrived in the fullness of time, without blemish and without spot, the male of the first year in the perfection of His humanity and offered Himself once for all so that every morning and every evening of every life lived under the blood is covered.

We thank You that He is not merely a memory on an altar but the standing Lamb at the centre of the throne, bearing the marks of slaughter. Help us today to live as people who are under the blood; passed over by judgment, cleansed from the leprosy of sin, restored to full fellowship, and walking toward the day when we will hear your voice. In Christ’s name, amen.
